content: 1. The behavior of hand hygiene, as outlined in the good practice statement section of this chapter, is critical for infection prevention and control (IPC). The Guideline Development Group (GDG) emphasized the importance of implementing the World Health Organization (WHO) standards for the adequate number and proper placement of hand hygiene facilities in all healthcare settings. 2. WHO recommends that water, soap, single-use or clean reusable towels, and alcohol-based hand rub dispensers should be available in all key areas of healthcare facilities, including points of care and all toilet facilities. This ensures adherence to good practices and compliance with the WHO’s “5 Moments for Hand Hygiene.” 3. Regarding handwashing stations, WHO advises a minimum of one handwashing basin for every 10 beds and the availability of alcohol-based hand rubs at each point of care. 4. Hand hygiene is considered the cornerstone of clinical practice, essential for preventing healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and limiting the spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR). These practices are recognized as the gold standard and are implemented in many countries worldwide. 5. A multimodal strategy is the internationally accepted approach to achieving behavioral change in hand hygiene. One of the five core elements of the WHO hand hygiene improvement strategy focuses on the work system, including infrastructure and materials, to facilitate compliance at the point of care. 6. Evidence reviews were conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of IPC programs. One key component identified was the availability of materials and equipment to perform IPC practices at the point of care. The primary outcomes assessed were the impact on HAIs and hand hygiene compliance. 7. Eleven studies were included in the review, with six specifically addressing hand hygiene. These studies highlighted the importance of having hand hygiene products, such as alcohol-based hand rubs, easily accessible at the point of care, ideally within arm’s reach of where patient care or treatment occurs. 8. The placement of hand rub dispensers at the point of care was identified as a determinant of hand hygiene compliance. One study demonstrated a significant improvement in hand hygiene behavior among anesthesiologists when provided with pocket bottles of alcohol-based hand rub. 9. Limited access to hand hygiene facilities was noted as a source of frustration for healthcare workers in one qualitative study. Additionally, customized insertion kits for central venous catheters and pre-stocked carts were shown to reduce central line-associated bloodstream infections in three studies. 10. Improved prescribing of isolation measures was associated with the use of electronic reminders for doctors when ordering isolation precautions for patients meeting specific criteria. 11. The GDG concluded that ensuring the availability and appropriate placement of hand hygiene materials and equipment at the point of care is essential for supporting proper hand hygiene practices. 12. The GDG identified the need for more high-quality research to evaluate the impact of system changes on reducing HAIs and AMR, as well as changes in practices. Further investigation into the local production of alcohol-based hand rubs, including quality control and acceptance, is also recommended. 13. The guidelines aim to improve the quality and safety of healthcare, patient outcomes, and the safety of healthcare workers. Adoption of the recommendations and adaptation of existing IPC approaches at national and facility levels are key to success. 14. The inclusion of IPC core components in national action plans for AMR is crucial for achieving strategic objectives outlined in the AMR Global Action Plan adopted by WHO Member States. 15. Dissemination and implementation of these guidelines are essential at international, national, and local levels. Success depends on the perceived relevance of the guidelines by IPC leads and the effective integration of IPC with health security, public health, supply chain, and other critical systems. 16. National IPC programs should support local programs by setting standards, fostering training and recruitment of infection preventionists, ensuring regular provision of IPC supplies, and coordinating activities with local IPC programs. 17. Implementation of the guidelines requires a robust strategy and adaptation to local contexts. WHO is developing resources to accompany the guidelines, including strategies for implementation in resource-limited settings and comprehensive IPC training packages. 18. Dissemination of the guidelines will occur through various mechanisms, including WHO campaigns, collaborating centers, regional offices, ministries of health, and professional associations. Social media and mobile health technologies will also be explored as supplementary dissemination tools. 19. An evaluation framework will be developed to measure the implementation of the guidelines. Mechanisms will track the number of countries incorporating IPC core components into their national programs, requests for technical assistance, and adaptation or translation efforts. 20. WHO plans to review and update the guidelines every 3–5 years, informed by lessons learned from previous dissemination and implementation efforts.
